title: Price-quality Heuristic (Why We Think Expensive = Better)
description: In the absence of other information, people use price as a shortcut to judge quality. A higher price often raises expectations and actually enhances perceived taste, effectiveness, or value—even when the product is identical.
shortDescription: In the absence of other information, people use price as a shortcut to judge quality. A higher price often raises expectations and actually enhances perceived taste, effectiveness, or value—even when the product is identical.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: In the absence of other information, people use price as a shortcut to judge quality. A higher price often raises expectations and actually enhances perceived taste, effectiveness, or value—even when the product is identical.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A $50 wine tastes better than the same wine in a $10 bottle.
A placebo painkiller at a higher price provides more relief than the same placebo at a lower price.
A consultant who charges $500/hour is assumed to be more competent than one who charges $100/hour, regardless of outcomes.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Choosing the more expensive option in a product category to “be safe.”
Bragging about the cost of a purchase as a proxy for quality.
Dismissing low‑priced competitors as “cheap” without evaluating the product.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “It’s expensive, so it must be good.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You automatically filter products by price, looking only at the high end.
You’ve never actually compared the expensive version with the cheaper version in a blind test.
You justify a purchase by its price, not its performance.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The price‑quality heuristic is a mental shortcut for when direct quality information is absent or hard to obtain. Rao and Monroe (1989) showed that price has a positive effect on perceived quality, especially for unfamiliar products. Placebo pricing effects are well‑documented.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When possible, do a blind comparison or read independent reviews that isolate quality from price.
Ask: “If this product were 50% cheaper, would I still believe it’s good?”
Recognize that in some categories (commodities, generic drugs), price is completely disconnected from quality.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Dismissing the heuristic entirely; sometimes price does correlate with quality (e.g., ingredients, materials). The error is using price as the only signal.
Over‑adjusting and always buying the cheapest option, missing genuine quality.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A marketing agency pitches a branding package at $50,000. The client hesitates. The agency rep says, “We can do it for $15,000 if you want something basic.” The client suddenly feels the $50,000 option is the “real” one and signs. The $15,000 anchor made the higher price seem like a quality signal, not just a cost.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Price is a price tag, not a report card. The number doesn’t tell you how good something is—it tells you how much you’re willing to believe.
